quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

Here is what you need to do — six research items, all targeting external sites (primarily Archion):

---

### Background
Katharina Seeger (I1) was born about 1843 in Baiersbronn, Württemberg, and there are no parent records in the project yet. FamilySearch holds no digitized records for this parish, so all searches go through **Archion**, a paid German archive site that has scanned Baiersbronn's Protestant registers — but they are browse-only (not name-indexed), so you must page through them manually.

---

### The 6 Plan Items (in order)

| # | Type | Record Set | Site | Notes |
|---|------|-----------|------|-------|
| **pli_001** | Church | Baiersbronn Protestant Parish, baptisms 1840–1847 | Archion | **Start here.** Katharina's own baptism entry names father, mother (with maiden name), date, and godparents — the most direct answer. |
| **pli_002** | Church | Baiersbronn Familienregister (household ledger), 1800–1870 | Archion | Lists a couple and all their children on one page — often faster than scanning year-by-year baptism entries. |
| **pli_003** | Church | Baiersbronn Protestant Parish, marriages 1830–1845 | Archion | Parents' marriage entry — gives mother's maiden name and confirms the couple. |
| **pli_004** | Church | Baiersbronn death/burial register, 1843–1900 | Archion | Katharina's burial entry as a fallback if the baptism page is missing or damaged; may state parentage or age. |
| **pli_005** | Church (FAN) | Baiersbronn baptisms, 1835–1855 | Archion | Siblings' baptisms — each entry repeats both parents' names and identifies godparent neighbors/kin. |
| **pli_006** | Church | Württemberg church records, c. 1840–1847 | Ancestry | Name-searchable fallback for pli_001; search surname Seeger/Seger, birth ~1843, Baiersbronn/Freudenstadt. Requires Ancestry subscription. |

---

### How to Start

1. Go to the **Archion Baiersbronn parish page**:
   [https://www.archion.de/de/alle-archive/baden-wuerttemberg/evangelisches-archiv-baden-und-wuerttemberg-wuerttemberg/dekanat-freudenstadt/baiersbronn](https://www.archion.de/de/alle-archive/baden-wuerttemberg/evangelisches-archiv-baden-und-wuerttemberg-wuerttemberg/dekanat-freudenstadt/baiersbronn)
2. Navigate to the **baptism register (Taufbuch) for the early 1840s**.
3. Browse for an entry for **"Katharina Seeger"** born around 1843.
4. The entry should list her **father's name**, her **mother's name** (usually with maiden name), and the birth date.
5. Capture the page and upload it when you find it — route the result to **search-external-sites** for logging.

All six items are external-site searches, so hand them off to **search-external-sites** when ready to execute.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Per loc_001, Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia through 1875; search variant spellings 'Flyn' and 'Flyun' as well.

The Schuylkill County Deed Records 1815-1900 (image group 007936752) is 22% record-searchable, making it name-searchable for a substantial portion of the entries. In Catholic parish practice of this era, the marriage register sometimes listed the contracting parties' parents' names, particularly where the priest gathered information for the banns. Patrick's marriage window is approximately 1865-1908 (born ~1845, died 1908). Identifying his wife also traces the family line that produced the son-in-law informant on the death certificate (James Brown), who may hold additional oral knowledge of Patrick's origins. The Schuylkill County Naturalization Records 1849-1915 (image group 007936750) are browse-only (personCount 0). Post-1906 petitions for naturalization required a detailed declaration including the names of wife and children; pre-1906 records are sparser but still list the declarant's name, origin, and arrival date. If Thomas Flynn naturalized and listed Patrick among his children, this would be independent documentary evidence of the parent-child relationship. Thomas was born ~1818 in Ireland, making naturalization plausible any time from the 1850s onward. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

items.notes: Supported only by the occupation/location change visible across log_001 (1870, farmer, elsewhere) and log_002 (1882, miner, Schuylkill County). No direct record of the move's cause -- no land transaction, employment record, letter, or newspaper item -- has been found for Michael himself yet.

entry.rationale: The 1870 census (log_001) found Michael as a farmer outside Schuylkill County; the 1882 county directory (log_002) found him as a miner there. The 1880 US Census (collection 1417683, name-searchable) falls squarely in the gap. If Michael appears in Schuylkill County in 1880, the move predates the directory; if he is elsewhere and still farming, the transition to mining occurred in 1880-1882. His 1880 occupation — farmer vs. miner — directly tests whether coal-mining drew him to the county or whether he had already begun that transition elsewhere. Searching surname variants Sheehan, Shehan, and Shehane alongside Sheahan is necessary.

Patrick Sheahan (I2, Michael's sibling) purchased land in Schuylkill County in 1875 — seven years before Michael's 1882 directory appearance (tree fact F4, Deed Book 42, p. 118, source S1). Chain migration following an already-established sibling is an equally plausible motivation alongside purely economic pull from the mines. Searching the 1880 US Census (collection 1417683, name-searchable) for Patrick Sheahan in Schuylkill County reveals what this item tells about Michael: whether Michael was already living in Patrick's household before 1882, what Patrick's own occupation was (miner or not), and whether the brothers were part of the same coal-community settlement before Michael formally appears under his own name. This is a FAN item required by the migration-motivation question type.

The 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable) covers 1708-1985 across county Catholic and Protestant parishes. Irish miners in Schuylkill County predominantly worshipped in Roman Catholic parishes under the Diocese of Philadelphia (loc_001). A marriage, baptism of a child, or first communion record in Michael's name would establish: a minimum arrival date in the county, the specific parish and colliery district where he settled, and named godparents or witnesses who are FAN contacts from the same Irish mining community. This collection may record an arrival date earlier than the 1882 directory if Michael came before that year. Variants Sheehan and Shehan should be searched.

Volume 007936750, Schuylkill County naturalization records 1849-1915, browse-only (personCount 0). Irish emigrants to the Pennsylvania anthracite region commonly filed a declaration of intent ('first papers') in the county court of common pleas within 2-5 years of arrival. Michael's declaration, if filed, would record his country of birth, the date he first arrived in the United States, and his occupation at time of filing. His stated occupation at filing — miner or another trade — directly tests whether coal-mining was the reason for his presence in Schuylkill County. Pre-1906 Pennsylvania has no civil vital registration (loc_001), making naturalization one of the few record types that captures an immigrant's own statement of origin and arrival. Browse-only: examine images in the 1878-1895 window for Sheahan and Sheehan entries.

Pennsylvania's Bureau of Mines published annual colliery inspection reports from 1870 onward. Each report covers Schuylkill County collieries individually, recording the superintendent, workforce size, and the names of workers killed or injured in accidents. If Michael Sheahan appears in a fatality, injury, or employment roster entry for a specific colliery, that is the most direct available evidence for the coal-mining employment motivation: it names him, his employer, and the mine. These volumes are held by the Pennsylvania State Archives in Harrisburg and selected volumes are available through HathiTrust Digital Library. A positive finding would resolve hypothesis h_001 (anthracite coal-mining employment) with direct documentation.

The 1900 US Census (collection 1325221, name-searchable) asked each person their year of immigration and number of years naturalized. If Michael was foreign-born, the 1900 entry gives his immigration year — establishing whether he came directly to Schuylkill County or settled elsewhere first — and his naturalization status, cross-checking the naturalization record at item 4. His 1900 occupation (still miner, or changed?) and county of residence confirm continued presence in the anthracite region and corroborate the overall migration timeline. This is the earliest federal census carrying immigration-year data. Variant spellings Sheehan and Shehan should be searched.

Volume 007936752, Schuylkill County deed records 1815-1900, 22% record-searchable. The locality guide (loc_001) notes that coal-region laborers typically leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright, so an absence of a deed in Michael's name is consistent with his role as a wage-miner tenant. However, any deed or lease in his name would confirm when he acquired property in the county and from whom; a mining company as grantor would directly corroborate that his housing was tied to mining employment. Patrick's 1875 purchase from James Kelly (source S1) shows the family engaged the county deed system; Kelly may also be a community FAN connection. Run the name search on the 22% indexed portion first; browse images for the 1882-1895 range if the index misses entries.

Volume 007936751, Schuylkill County church records 1842-1895 (English and German languages), browse-only (personCount 0). If the name-searchable church collection at item 3 returns no results for Sheahan or Sheehan, this unindexed volume covering overlapping years provides the fallback. German-language entries reflect Lutheran and Reformed congregations; Irish Catholic entries are in English. Browsing the Catholic register sections in the 1878-1892 window may surface Michael's marriage or a child's baptism that confirms the settlement date, and is especially worth examining if item 3's indexed collection omits some parishes.

**Question:** q_001 — "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

---

## Tree Survey Findings

- **Patrick Flynn (I1):** born ~1845 Ireland (the objective's "Pennsylvania" disagrees — the tree's 1850 census entry gives Ireland; the death certificate, pli_004, will settle this), died 1908-03-12 Schuylkill County, PA. Sources S1 (1850 census, dwelling 84) and S3 (PA Death Cert no. 4521) on the person.
- **Thomas Flynn (I2):** born ~1818 Ireland. No death date or death place in the tree. No sources attached to Thomas's own record.

- S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records, Register of Wills) is in the tree source list but is not cited on any person, fact, or relationship, and no assertions from it exist.

---

## Plan pl_002 — 10 Items in Execution Order

| # | Item | Type | Repository / Collection | Purpose |
|---|------|------|------------------------|---------|
| pli_004 | PA Death Cert (1908) | vital_record | FamilySearch collection 2255317 | Extract parentage data from Patrick's death cert (S3 cited but never extracted for q_001); likely names both parents |
| pli_005 | 1860 US Census | census | FamilySearch collection 1473181 | Second co-enumeration of Patrick in Thomas's household; confirm S2 with a formal q_001 assertion |
| pli_006 | PA Probate Records | probate | FamilySearch collection 1999196 + image group 007936749 | Thomas's will naming Patrick as son = direct parentage evidence; dower release names the mother |
| pli_007 | Schuylkill Church Records (indexed) | church | FamilySearch SYNTH-PA-CHURCH | Mother's maiden name unknown — search Thomas Flynn as groom for parents' marriage |
| pli_008 | Schuylkill Church Register (browse) | church | FamilySearch vol. 007936751 | Fallback image browse if pli_007 indexed search misses the record |
| pli_009 | 1870 US Census | census | FamilySearch collection 1438024 | Find wife's name if she survived; identify other children |
| pli_010 | 1880 US Census | census | FamilySearch collection 1417683 | 1880 schedule records relationship to head — strongest co-enumeration corroboration |
| pli_011 | Schuylkill Naturalization Records | immigration | FamilySearch vol. 007936750 | Post-1870 petitions name wife, children with ages, and Irish county of origin |
| pli_012 | Civil War Soldiers Index | military | FamilySearch collection 1910717 | Patrick age 16–20 during war; enlistment/pension papers may name parents |
| pli_013 | Schuylkill Deed Records | land | FamilySearch vol. 007936752 | FAN search; dower releases directly name the mother; neighbor network |

**Breadth check:** Seven record-type categories (vital, census ×3, probate, church ×2, naturalization, military, land/FAN) across three repositories.

## Birthplace Note
The project objective says "born ca. 1845 in Pennsylvania" but the tree records **Ireland** as Patrick's birthplace (derived from the 1850 census). This is a factual inconsistency in the project setup; **pli_004** (the death certificate) will clarify which is correct.

Execute the name-searchable FamilySearch searches — starting with pli_004 (death certificate collection), then pli_005 (1860 census), then pli_007 (church records) — followed by image-browse films for pli_006 (probate), pli_008 (church), and pli_011 (naturalization). Use **search-records** for all FamilySearch items; use **search-records** in browse mode for the image-group items. Execution was not pre-authorized — confirmation is needed before proceeding.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Patrick's 1908 death certificate (S3 in project tree, citing Pennsylvania Death Certificates) is referenced in relationship R1 but no parentage data has been formally extracted for q_001. Collection 2255317 (Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906-1968) is name-searchable. Per loc_001, Pennsylvania statewide civil death registration began in 1906, so Patrick's March 1908 death falls within that period. A death certificate typically names both parents; the informant's proximity to the family determines evidential quality. This is the most direct surviving American record likely to name Thomas as father and to supply the mother's name — the key unknown not yet established. Note: the tree records Patrick's birthplace as Ireland (from the 1850 census entry), not Pennsylvania as stated in the objective; the death certificate may confirm which is correct.

The 1860 census (S2 in project tree) is cited in relationship R1 at quality 2 but no q_001 assertion has been formally extracted from it. Collection 1473181 (United States Census, 1860) is name-searchable. Finding Patrick (then ~15) again in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household is a second co-enumeration corroborating the parentage inference established by a_004 (1850 census). The 1860 census records birthplace for each person; Patrick's Ireland birthplace, consistent with a_004, further confirms identity. Search both Flynn and Flinn.

S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records, Register of Wills) is listed in the project tree sources but no assertions have been extracted from it for q_001. Thomas Flynn (born ~1818 Ireland) would plausibly have died between 1860 and ~1900; the date range is bounded by Thomas's estimated lifespan, not Patrick's research window. Per loc_001, probate records are held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994) is browse-only (personCount 0); volume_search also returned image group 007936749 (Schuylkill probate, 1851-1930, browse-only). A will naming Patrick as a son, or an intestate administration listing him as next of kin, is direct parentage evidence. Pennsylvania law required a wife to separately dower-release real property — any deed Thomas signed would name his wife, supplying the mother's name.

Dedicated item for the parents' marriage — required for a parentage question. The mother's maiden name is entirely unknown; neither the tree nor any assertion names her. Thomas Flynn (born ~1818 Ireland) and his wife almost certainly married in Ireland before 1845 (Patrick was born there ~1845), so this Schuylkill search may not find the original marriage ceremony; however, a church marriage or recorded ceremony in Schuylkill County would supply the mother's name. Collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records, 1708-1985) is name-searchable. Search Thomas Flynn or Flinn as groom. This collection may also contain a baptism for a sibling of Patrick born in Schuylkill after the family emigrated, which would name both parents. A marriage record's date relative to Patrick's ~1845 birth corroborates Thomas as father but does not by itself prove Patrick is their child — that link still requires a record placing Patrick with the couple.

Fallback for pli_007. Volume 007936751 (Schuylkill County Church Records, 1842-1895) is browse-only (personCount 0), covering English- and German-language registers. If the indexed SYNTH-PA-CHURCH search for pli_007 finds no marriage or baptism record for Thomas Flynn, browse this image group page by page in the Catholic or Protestant registers for the Schuylkill coalfield townships where the family likely resided.

Thomas Flynn (born ~1818) would be ~52 in 1870. Collection 1438024 (United States Census, 1870) is name-searchable. Locating Thomas in 1870 shows whether he remained in Schuylkill County, who was still in his household (wife, other children), and whether Patrick had left home. A wife's name in the 1870 household would identify the mother. If Thomas died before 1870, his widow's household may name surviving children. Search Flynn and Flinn.

Thomas Flynn (born ~1818) would be ~62 in 1880. Collection 1417683 (United States Census, 1880) is name-searchable. Unlike the 1850 and 1860 schedules, the 1880 census explicitly states each person's relationship to the head of household, making a Thomas Flynn household entry considerably stronger corroboration of parentage than prior census co-enumeration. A wife living in 1880 would be named. Search Flynn and Flinn.

Volume 007936750 (Schuylkill County Naturalization Records, 1849-1915) is browse-only (personCount 0). Thomas Flynn, an Irish-born immigrant present in Schuylkill County by 1850, would likely have filed a declaration of intent and petition for naturalization. Petitions filed from the 1870s onward routinely name the petitioner's wife, children (with ages), and county of origin in Ireland. Identifying Thomas's home county opens a path to Irish baptismal and marriage registers. The date range covers Thomas's plausible naturalization window; its bounds follow Thomas's estimated lifespan, not Patrick's own research window.

Patrick Flynn (born ~1845) was 16-20 years old during the Civil War. Collection 1910717 (United States Civil War Soldiers Index, 1861-1865) is name-searchable. Union enlistment papers record age, birthplace, and occupation; pension applications filed afterward sometimes include depositions by relatives or neighbors naming parents. Even a negative result closes this source type and its associated pension files. Search Flynn and Flinn.

FAN item required for a parentage question. Volume 007936752 (Schuylkill County Deed Records, 1815-1900) is name-searchable (22% of records indexed). Thomas Flynn's deed transactions would name grantors, grantees, and boundary neighbors — all potential kin or associates in the Irish immigrant anthracite mining community. Pennsylvania law required a wife to separately dower-release any real property Thomas sold; any such deed names the mother directly. Witnesses to deeds are frequently relatives. Search Flynn and Flinn as grantor and grantee.

- Assertion a_003: name "M J Wood" from the 7 Jan 1869 Smith County TX marriage record (src_002); quality secondary; informant bias note flags that Wood is established as her birth surname only if the 1869 Lanham marriage was her first — not yet established
- Assertion a_004: married W F Lanham 7 Jan 1869, Smith County TX — primary quality
- No parents recorded in the tree; no parentIds on I2

**Plan pl_001 — 6 items, q_002:**

- **pli_001** | census | Blount County, Alabama | 1860 | FamilySearch | — A pre-existing tree source places an "M M Wood" household in Blount County 1860; census volume 005154190 is 99% name-indexed; collection 1473181 is name-searchable. Finding Martha in that household confirms Wood as her birth surname and names her parents.

- **pli_002** | vital_record (marriage) | Smith County, Texas | 1857–1869 | FamilySearch | — 100% name-indexed; searches for any Smith County marriage of Martha / M J / Mattie before January 1869 (including to a man named Wood). Resolves the critical dependency: if Wood was a married name, the Wood-family searches may miss her birth family entirely.

- **pli_003** | vital_record (marriage) | Blount County, Alabama | 1840–1875 | FamilySearch | — collection 1598408, name-searchable; finds the parents' marriage and the mother's maiden name if item 1 confirms the Wood household; window also catches any early Alabama marriage of Martha herself.

- **pli_004** | census | Texas, United States | 1870 | FamilySearch | — collection 1438024; confirms Martha's age and Georgia birthplace as Mrs. Lanham; FAN-cluster sweep of neighboring households may include Wood-surname migrants who traveled alongside Martha from Alabama.

- **pli_005** | census | Texas, United States | 1880 | FamilySearch | — collection 1417683; finds Martha as Mrs. Neal; the 1880 census recorded each person's parents' birthplaces, which corroborates or refines the Georgia origin and could support a future Georgia county search.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: The 1870 US Census (collection 1438024, name-searchable) falls squarely in the middle of the likely Doyle marriage period. Bridget (born ~1838 Ireland) would be ~32, and any children born between roughly 1858 and 1870 would appear in the household. The 1900 census fertility data (log_002) shows Bridget bore 9 children; this census is the highest-probability single source for naming multiple Doyle children at once, given that John Doyle died before the 1879 remarriage and most children were born in this window. The loc_001 locality guide confirms Schuylkill County as the relevant jurisdiction for the whole period.

The 1860 US Census (collection 1473181, name-searchable) captures the earliest Doyle children — those born in the late 1850s. Bridget (~22 in 1860) and John Doyle would appear as a young couple, and any children born by 1860 would be listed. Children who appear here but not in the 1870 household likely died young, and their names are part of the answer to the question. Searching under both Doyle and Halloran (in case the enumerator recorded the wife's surname) is warranted given Irish naming variation in the anthracite region.

The 1880 US Census (collection 1417683, name-searchable) comes one year after Bridget's 1879 remarriage to Martin Kearney (log_001). Any Doyle children still at home would appear in the Kearney household, listed under their Doyle surname or with a relationship note. Older Doyle children (born 1858–1865) may by 1880 have established their own households in the county, making a broader Schuylkill County name search important. The 1880 census is also the first to record each person's relationship to the head of household, which directly identifies which children remain with Bridget.

The 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable) holds 982,415 persons across 1708–1985. The loc_001 locality guide notes that Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County were under the Diocese of Philadelphia (archdiocese 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese. Baptism entries for children of John Doyle and Bridget Halloran/Doyle would name each child directly. Burial entries for children who died in infancy or childhood — seven to eight of the nine total — would appear here and yield names absent from the census. Both should be searched. The supplementary image group 007936751 (Schuylkill County Church Records, 1842–1895, 187 images) is browse-only (personCount 0) and serves as a supplement if the indexed collection has gaps.

The 1900 US Census (collection 1325221, name-searchable) was already searched for Bridget's Kearney household (log_002), confirming 2 surviving children. This item separately targets adult Doyle children who by 1900 would be ages ~22–42 and likely living in their own households in Schuylkill County. The 1900 census records birthplace and parents' birthplace — Ireland for both John Doyle and Bridget Halloran — which corroborates identity as their children. Searching for Doyle-surname households headed by a person of the right age and birthplace (Pennsylvania, born to Ireland-born parents) will surface surviving children not yet named.

The 1910 US Census (collection 1488411, name-searchable) extends coverage for surviving Doyle children, who by 1910 would be ages ~32–52. Any child identified in the 1900 census can be confirmed across this census, closing the decade and verifying survival. If a child is present in 1900 but absent in 1910, a death in the intervening decade directs a targeted death-certificate search. The 1910 census also captures any children who migrated within or out of Schuylkill County.

John Doyle died before Bridget's 1879 remarriage (log_001). His probate file — a will or letters of administration — would be held by the Schuylkill County Register of Wills, available from 1811 (loc_001). A will naming his children, or an administration listing heirs, is the most legally authoritative evidence of which children John Doyle acknowledged. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0); image group 007936749 (Schuylkill County Probate Records, 1851–1930, 412 images) is also browse-only (personCount 0), requiring an image-by-image review of the probate dockets for the 1858–1879 window. Date range is bounded by the estimated earliest marriage year and the confirmed pre-1879 death.

Pennsylvania civil death registration began in 1906 (loc_001). Any Doyle child who survived past 1906 and died in Pennsylvania would have a death certificate whose informant section names their parents — directly recording John Doyle and Bridget Halloran. Bridget's children born 1858–1878 would be ages 28–80 across 1906–1940; this window captures most natural-lifespan deaths for the surviving cohort. Searching on the Doyle surname with Ireland-born parents narrows the field. Variant spellings (Doyel, O'Doyle) should be attempted.

Seven to eight of Bridget's nine children died before 1900, most likely in infancy or childhood (loc_001 notes that Pennsylvania civil registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 child deaths rely on church burial or cemetery evidence). FindAGrave's Schuylkill County coverage may show Doyle-surname burials clustered at the same section or plot as John Doyle or Bridget Halloran, identifying children not captured in the indexed church records. This item serves as a fallback if pli_004 (church records) does not name all the deceased children.

FAN item — Ellen Doyle (I3) is the one identified child of John Doyle and Bridget Halloran. Her marriage record was found incidentally (log_003) and confirms her parents. Her death certificate, if she died after Pennsylvania civil registration began in 1906, would name her parents again and potentially identify the informant as a sibling or other family member whose name leads to additional Doyle children. This is a targeted search for Ellen specifically, distinct from the broader Doyle-surname death-certificate sweep in pli_008. An informant who is a sibling is direct evidence of another Doyle child.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.
